summary: An informative overview of how legacy applications can be made to work with the Host Identity Protocol (HIP). HIP adds a cryptographic name space for hosts, a new address family from the application's point of view, but it may take a long time before applications understand it. This document looks at ways to bridge the gap.

eli5.summary: A new kind of ID card is useless if old shops do not recognize it. This explains how to let older programs use the new ID system without rewriting them.

questions: how to use hip with legacy applications
subtitle: Making new cryptographic host IDs work with unmodified applications.

tldr.problem: HIP adds a cryptographic namespace for host identifiers, but applications will continue using IP addresses for years. Systems become HIP-aware long before applications do, creating a deployment gap.
tldr.mechanism: The system can transparently intercept IP address usage at the API level or DNS resolution level, mapping them to HIP identifiers without changing applications.
tldr.outcome: Legacy applications can benefit from HIP's cryptographic authentication and mobility without modification, easing the incremental transition to HIP-aware systems.

today: RFC 5338 provides guidance for implementers and remains relevant for HIP research and experimental deployments. The Host Identity Protocol itself remains experimental and has not achieved widespread deployment, but the techniques described here remain applicable for systems exploring incremental HIP adoption.

sections.title: Bridging HIP and Legacy Applications
sections.content:
HIP (Host Identity Protocol) introduces a new cryptographic namespace for host names, separate from IP addresses. In a fully HIP-enabled system, applications would explicitly ask the system to send packets to a peer by its unique cryptographic identity, not its IP address. However, there will be a long transition period where systems support HIP but applications do not.

This document explores practical techniques for making HIP work with unmodified applications that still use IP-based APIs. It is not a normative specification, but rather a guide for implementers handling real-world incremental deployment.
sections.eli5: New systems can speak HIP, but old programs still expect IP addresses. The document explains how systems can bridge this gap without rewriting the old programs.

sections.title: Key Concepts in HIP for Legacy Apps
sections.content:
HIP introduces two main ways to name hosts: the Host Identity Tag (HIT), a 128-bit hash of a public key, and the Local Scope Identifier (LSI), a 32- or 128-bit local mapping. Both can be used where IP addresses normally appear.

Legacy applications use IP addresses in several ways. Some use them briefly as handles for DNS queries, others cache them for long-lived connections, and some pass them to other parties as referrals or store them in logs. Each use case has different implications when HITs or LSIs are substituted.
sections.eli5: A HIT is like a person's real ID; an LSI is like a local nickname. Old programs treat both as regular addresses, but they secretly point to cryptographic identities instead.

sections.title: Transparent System-Level Enablement
sections.content:
One approach is to enable HIP without the user or application knowing. The system can intercept an application's connect() call to an IP address and map it to a HIT internally. Another option is to interpose a local DNS agent that returns LSIs or HITs instead of IP addresses when they are available.

If the system maps IP-to-HIT at the policy level (such as based on firewall rules), the application sees no change but the packets are authenticated. If the resolver returns LSIs, the system maintains a mapping between the LSI and the true HIT. The challenge is that applications may cache LSIs long-term or pass them to other systems that cannot resolve them back.
sections.eli5: The operating system can silently intercept old programs asking for IP addresses and secretly use HIP instead, or the system can trick the DNS resolver into giving out HIP identities disguised as addresses.

sections.title: User-Controlled HIP Invocation
sections.content:
Sometimes a user wants to explicitly choose to use HIP for a specific connection. An application might accept a HIT or LSI directly in place of an IP address, or the user can provide a modified domain name like HIP-www.example.com to signal the resolver to return HIP identifiers. When users connect directly to a HIT, the security is stronger: the application explicitly asks to communicate with a specific cryptographic identity.

Direct HIT use has tradeoffs. HITs are flat and harder for humans to remember than domain names or IPv6 addresses. A separate service is needed to map HITs to reachable IP addresses. And if an application makes referrals to other hosts, those hosts must either support HIP or understand how to resolve the HIT.
sections.eli5: Users can hand an old program a HIT instead of an IP address, or use a special DNS name prefix to ask for HIP identities. The system then secretly uses HIP for that connection.

sections.title: Servers and Local Address Management
sections.content:
Server applications typically bind to a wildcard IP address to accept connections on any interface. When HIP is used, a server with multiple HITs must decide which HIT to advertise in DNS or configuration. If different HITs are announced but the server binds to a wildcard, the response packets may come from a different HIT than the client expected, causing the client to drop them.

A HIP implementation can use virtual interfaces with assigned HITs, making it easier for the application layer to work with them. It can also return HITs or LSIs from DNS lookups of local addresses. The simplest approach for legacy UDP servers is to announce only the default HIT that matches outgoing packets.
sections.eli5: Servers that listen on many addresses need to announce which one they actually use, or clients will be confused when responses come from an unexpected address.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
Different transition techniques offer different security guarantees. Manual IP-to-HIT configuration provides security similar to a non-HIP system with IPsec policies. Opportunistic HIP (initiating HIP with an unknown peer) is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks but resists connection hijacking. If DNS is secured with DNSSEC and HITs are stored in DNS, and the client trusts the DNSSEC signatures, security approaches that of TLS with certificates.

When applications use HITs, connections are automatically secured by the implicit channel bindings in HIP: either packets reach the holder of the corresponding private key or the handshake fails. Spoofing LSIs or HITs in logs and user interfaces can confuse administrators, so HIP implementations should log all identifiers alongside IP addresses and domain names for correlation.
sections.eli5: Using HITs is very secure: you know you are talking to the owner of that key, period. Using IP addresses with HIP is less certain but still better than plain IP. DNS security matters if you trust DNS.
